newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia ships out exports as trade surplus soars.
newsitem.headline: Australia ships out exports as trade surplus soars.

text.p: Australia was literally shipping out exports in May as the delivery of a navy frigate to New Zealand helped it achieve a record monthly trade surplus.

Data released on Tuesday showed the balance of goods and services was in surplus to the tune of A$873 million for the month, up a massive A$691 million, or 380 percent, on April's A$182 million surplus.

Australia is often criticised for its poor external account balances. But the Australian Bureau of Statistics said May's surplus was the highest it had on records going back to 1977. Within the surplus exports of goods rose by 6.3 percent in the month, while imports of goods fell 5.4 percent.
The main reason for the jump was the export to New Zealand of a A$500 million navy frigate, but economists said it could not be completely discounted as a one-off.
"This is unlikely to be repeated, of course, but it is still a genuine export, so not all of the gloss should be rubbed off today's news," Bankers Trust Australia economists said in a commentary.

"The balance on goods and services remains in good shape, with the maintenance of surpluses helping in the long run adjustment to a lower current account deficit," added economists from Citibank Australia.
In any case, it was a nice change for Australia to be on the export side of a one-off transaction. Australia normally imports rather than exports capital goods.
"The one-off coming this way makes a change," said UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts, who said that while it would be positive for growth, it had few policy implications.
The cumulative surplus of A$1.055 billion over April and May had ensured that net exports would make a solid contribution to second quarter gross domestic product (GDP), he said.
"(But) because it's so much a one-off I don't think that it'll make any difference to the way the Reserve Bank reads economic activity at present," Roberts added.

Australia has now only had four monthly trade deficits over the past 15 months, a figure that analysts said was all the more imporessive given the strong appreciation of the Australian dollar over 1996.

"The weakening of the exchange rate in recent months, and the expectation of continuing weakness in the coming quarters, suggests that export growth will strengthen further and the run of surpluses in the goods and services balance will continue for some time yet," economists at Nomura Australia said.
Not all were as optimistic, pointing to the impact on rural exports of a forecast drought, and the prospect of stronger domestic growth later this year leading to increased imports.
Some analysts also saw signs of weakness in the data, despite the huge surplus, that remain supportive of calls for a rate cut.
Imports of goods and services are at their lowest level this year, a sign of continuing subdued demand in the economy.
Imports of capital goods, sometimes used as indicator of business investment, fell 12.6 percent in the month.
"The import numbers are consistent with the anecdotal evidence of the economy growing at a pace well below potential and one that could do with some kickstarting," the Citibank economists said.
